Empirical Research Plan ― The Long-Run Effects of the Colonial Mining Mita in Peru
==================================================================================

1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------
Method: Sharp geographic regression-discontinuity design (RDD).

Rationale  
•  Treatment (forced-labor obligation) was assigned exclusively by a legally fixed geographic boundary drawn in 1573; location relative to that boundary is therefore an exogenous forcing variable.  
•  Outcomes are observed more than 400 years later, so a panel or DiD design is impossible.  
•  The boundary is highly irregular and traverses very similar Andean topography on both sides, limiting omitted-variable concerns.  
•  The density of districts near the cutoff is adequate (≈ 500), allowing precise local comparisons.

2. Treatment and Control
------------------------
Treatment variable  
Tᵢ = 1 if district i’s population-weighted centroid lies inside Toledo’s 1573 mita catchment; 0 otherwise.

Control group  
Districts whose centroids fall just outside the mita boundary.

Running variable  
Signed distance in kilometers from district centroid to the closest point on the mita boundary:  
Rᵢ = (distance outside) – (distance inside).  
Thus Rᵢ = 0 at the boundary; Rᵢ < 0 for treated; Rᵢ > 0 for controls.

Cutoff  
c = 0 km.

Timing  
Institution started 1573, abolished 1812. For design purposes the “event” is assignment in 1573; treatment is permanently “on” for treated districts from that moment forward.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes: In the absence of mita assignment, expected present-day outcomes would vary smoothly with distance to the boundary.  
– Plausible because the boundary followed arbitrary mountain ridges and rivers, not pre-existing economic divisions, and pre-colonial ethnic and ecological zones straddled the line.

A2. No precise sorting/manipulation of the running variable: Communities could not choose their side of the line in 1573, and large-scale migration in response to the mita was heavily restricted by Spanish authorities.  
– Plausible given coercion and the fact that the boundary was unknown to most indigenous communities.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): Outcomes in one district are not affected by the mita status of another, at least within the estimation window.  
– Reasonable because colonial obligations were organized at the district (repartimiento) level, and modern spillovers decay with distance.

A4. Correct functional form/local polynomial within chosen bandwidth: With sufficiently narrow symmetric bandwidths and linear trends, bias is minimized.  
– Can be checked empirically.

4. Threats to Identification and Remedies
-----------------------------------------
T1. Geographic covariate discontinuities (elevation, ruggedness, soil quality) exactly at the boundary.  
•  Test: Balance checks and local-RDD plots of covariates.  
•  Remedy: Include flexible controls (elevation, slope, ruggedness, distance to Potosí/Cusco) interacted with polynomial in Rᵢ.

T2. Post-abolition migration or selective municipal creation that re-orders population relative to the boundary.  
•  Test: Compare 1876 and 1940 census ethnic/language composition across the cutoff.  
•  Remedy: Restrict to pre-1900 district boundaries (historical GIS), or instrument modern outcomes with historical population-weighted centroids.

T3. Measurement error in district centroids or boundary shapefile causing mis-classification.  
•  Test: Monte-Carlo perturbation of centroids ±5 km.  
•  Remedy: Drop districts whose centroid is <2 km from the line (fuzzy buffer); show robustness to alternative distance measures (min point-in-polygon distance).

5. R Code Outline
-----------------
```r
# Load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)          # GIS
library(rdrobust)    # RDD
library(fixest)      # regression
library(modelsummary)

# 1. Data loading --------------------------------------------------------
enaho   <- read_csv("enaho_households.csv")          # household outcomes
districts <- st_read("peru_district_shapefiles.shp") # polygons w/ centroids
mita_bd   <- st_read("mita_boundary_1573.shp")

# 2. Variable construction ----------------------------------------------
# Centroids
districts <- districts %>% 
  mutate(centroid = st_centroid(geometry)) %>% 
  st_as_sf()

# Signed distance to boundary (negative = inside)
signed_dist <- st_distance(districts$centroid, mita_bd) %>% as.numeric()
inside      <- st_within(districts$centroid, mita_bd, sparse = FALSE)[,1]
districts   <- districts %>% 
  mutate(R = ifelse(inside, -signed_dist, signed_dist),
         mita = ifelse(inside, 1, 0))

# Merge household data
data <- enaho %>% 
  left_join(districts %>% st_drop_geometry(), by = "district_id") %>% 
  mutate(log_cons = log(real_consumption))

# 3. Main specification: local linear RDD -------------------------------
# Bandwidth: Imbens-Kalyanaraman
bw <- IKbandwidth(data$R, data$mita)

# Household-level sharp RD with district clustering
rd_main <- feols(log_cons ~ mita + R | 0 | 0 | district_id,
                 data = data %>% filter(abs(R) <= bw))

# Summary
etable(rd_main)

# Alternative: rdrobust (bias-corrected)
rd_rob <- rdrobust(y = data$log_cons, x = data$R, c = 0,
                   cutoff = 0, p = 1, kernel = "triangular")

summary(rd_rob)

# 4. Covariate balance robustness check ---------------------------------
covs <- c("elevation","rugged","slope","dist_cusco")
balance <- map(covs, ~ rdrobust(y = districts[[.x]],
                                x = districts$R, p = 1))
map(balance, summary)

# 5. Sensitivity to bandwidth -------------------------------------------
bw_seq <- seq(10, 80, by = 10)  # km
sens <- map_dfr(bw_seq, ~ {
  est <- feols(log_cons ~ mita + R | 0 | 0 | district_id,
               data = data %>% filter(abs(R) <= .x))
  tibble(bw = .x, coef = coef(est)["mita"], se = se(est)["mita"])
})
ggplot(sens, aes(bw, coef)) + geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = coef-1.96*se, ymax = coef+1.96*se))

```
6. Expected Results
-------------------
Theory suggests enduring negative effects inside the mita:  
•  Lower consumption by ≈ 10 – 15 percent (−0.10 to −0.16 log points).  
•  Higher stunting rates by 3 – 5 percentage points.  
•  Fewer kilometers of paved road per 1,000 km² and lower probability of a secondary school or health post.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)
-------------------------------------------
C1: Sharp, known cutoff exogenously determined …………………. 1  
C2: No sorting/manipulation around cutoff …………………………… 1  
C3: Covariate continuity around cutoff ………………………………… 0.8 (minor terrain breaks)  
C4: Robust to bandwidth & polynomial choices …………………… 0.8 (will test)  
C5: Adequate number of observations near cutoff ………………… 1  
Total (out of 5) ………………………………………………………………… 4.6  

Overall, the geographic RDD exploiting Toledo’s 1573 mita boundary provides a credible strategy to uncover the persistent causal impact of colonial forced labor on modern development outcomes in Peru.
